title: NJ OAL Initial Decision — OAL DKT. NO. TYP 968-14
text:
State of New Jersey
OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
INITIAL DECISION
OAL DKT. NO. TYP968-14
AGENCY DKT. NO. 2-10-
MICHAEL PRICE,
Petitioner,
v.
PUBLIC EMPLOYEES’
RETIREMENT SYSTEM,
Respondent.
______________________________
Alexander J. Wazeter, Esq., for petitioner (Helmer, Conley, Kasselman, P.A., attorneys)
Jane Lafferty, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (John J. Hoffman, Acting Attorney General of New Jersey,
attorney)
Record Closed: July 17, 2015 Decided: August 24, 2015
BEFORE WILLIAM TODD MILLER, ALJ:
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
3 On October 17, 2013, the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees’ Retirement System (Board or PERS) denied
petitioner’s application for accidental-disability retirement benefits. The Board concluded that petitioner met all requirements for
eligibility under the applicable accidental-disability retirement law except that petitioner’s accident was not undesigned and
unexpected and there was no actual accident or external happening. Petitioner contends that he is eligible for accidental-
disability retirement benefits as a result of seriously injuring his lumbar spine, requiring a multi-level fusion, when he fell on a wet
tile pool deck while he was stepping off bleachers. For the reason discussed below, the determination of the Board is reversed.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY

1
The petitioner requested a hearing, and the matter was filed at the Office of Administrative Law on January 24, 2014, to be
heard as a contested case pursuant to N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 to -15 and N.J.S.A. 52:14F-1 to -13. The matter was heard on
February 17, 2015, and May 26, 2015. Closing briefs were submitted, and the record closed on July 17, 2015.
FACTUAL SUMMARY
The date of the incident is July 13, 2011. Petitioner was fifty-three years old and was employed as a teaching assistant by the
Department of Children and Families (DCF). Petitioner has more than thirty-two years of creditable pension service.
Petitioner’s teaching-assistant duties included, but were not limited to, serving DCF “at-risk” youths in numerous
supervisory capacities. (J-2.) These youths included students from group homes and students with emotional problems.
Petitioner also acted as a gym monitor and supervised detentions.
3 On July 13, 2011, petitioner was assigned to assist in taking DCF students from the Cape May County location to the
Cape May County Special Services School District (Special Services) for a swimming classA. pproximately eighteen students
went to the Special Services indoor pool. A certified swim instructor was present and provided swimming instruction to most of
the students.
A few students refused to swim, and petitioner was assigned to them as an aide. The non-swimming students were
permitted to sit on the bleachers surrounding the pool deck. Petitioner described the bleachers as the old-fashioned wooden
gym bleachers with approximately eight seats or steps up to the top bleacher, which rests against the back wall. Petitioner and
some of the students walked up the bleachers and sat against the back wall while the remaining students were in the pool. The
students were in and out of the pool during the class, causing the pool deck to get wet.
Special Services had a fire drill approximately twenty minutes into the swimming class. The alarm sounded and the
children in the pool exited. Petitioner and his non-swimming students were guided down the bleachers, and the students were
escorted out of the pool area. Petitioner walked down the bleachers behind the students. When he reached the bottom of the
bleachers and placed his first foot on the pool deck, his foot went out from under him and he flipped into the air, landing on his
back. He hit the tile pool deck very hard. Petitioner struck his left pelvic area at around his belt line, and also landed on his
shoulder blade.
The swim instructor apparently heard the impact, and immediately came to petitioner’s assistance. Petitioner was treated
at the scene, but no emergency services were required. Petitioner returned to the DCF building with his students, by bus. He
then was taken to the hospital.
Petitioner was required to prepare a written statement of the incident. (P-1.) The statement provides as follows:
Students were swim-testing at the Special Services School District Pool.I was sitting with students
on bleachers when a fire-drill was executed. I stepped [off] the bleachers onto a wet floor. My feet
went completely out from under me. I landed hard enough to be heard by other staff on my upper left
buttocks and fell back, hitting my back shoulder blade on the bleacher.
Petitioner eventually was diagnosed with considerable injury to his lumbar spine in the area of L-5 through S-1. He underwent

surgery, during which a rod and four screws were inserted into his spine. His L-4, L-5 and S-1 vertebrae were fused together.
Petitioner’s testimony was credible, and reliably established facts that were not disputed by the Board. Therefore, they were
accepted for purposes of this record as the facts of the case.
LEGAL DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
Petitioner filed for accidental-disability retirement benefits pursuant to N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43. This statute provides in
relevant part:
A member who has not attained age 65 shall, upon the application of the head of the department in
which he is employed or upon his own application or the application of one acting in his behalf, be
retired by the board of trustees, if said employee is permanently and totally disabled as a direct
result of a traumatic event occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or
assigned duties, on an accidental disability allowance.
In Richardson v. Board of Trustees, Police & Firemen’s Retirement System (PFRS), 192 N.J. 189 (2007), the New Jersey
Supreme Court modified the standard to qualify for accidental-disability retirement. To obtain accidental-disability benefits, a
member must prove:
1. that he is permanently and totally disabled;
2. as a direct result of a traumatic event that is
a. identifiable as to time and place,
b. undesigned and
unexpected,[2]
and
c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease
that is aggravated or accelerated by the work);
3. that the traumatic event occurred during and as a result of the member’s regular or assigned
[3]
duties;
4. that the disability was not the result of the member’s willful negligence; and
5. that the member is mentally or physically incapacitated from performing his usual or any other
duty.

[Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13 (emphasis added).]
“Traumatic event” and “accident” are synonymous in the context of accidental-disability law. Id. at 210 (citing Russo v.
Teachers’ Pension & Annuity Fund, 62 N.J. 142, 152 (1973)). Thus, if the term “accident” is substituted for “traumatic event” in
N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43, eligibility is better understood, as the statute would read as follows:
A member who has not attained age 65 shall, upon the application of the head of the department in
which he is employed or upon his own application or the application of one acting in his behalf, be
retired by the board of trustees, if said employee is permanently and totally disabled as a direct
result of [an accident] occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or assigned
duties, on an accidental disability allowance.
The statute does not specify that the incident must have been “undesigned and unexpected,” which was one of the
Board’s stated reasons for denial of accidental disability. This is a judicially created or common-law phrase that has developed
over time as accidental-disability cases have been interpreted over the last forty years. Therefore, the meaning, purpose and
intent of the phrase “undesigned and unexpected” should be understood as the terms are defined and as the court has designed
the phrase to be used, particularly by the illustration provided by the Supreme Court in Richardson.
Richardson holds that a member suffering a career-ending injury that occurs during and as a result of the member’s
regular or assigned duties will be eligible for accidental-disability retirement, so long as the injury does not aggravate a
preexisting condition; the injury was not contrived; and the employee is permanently and totally disabled from the performance of
his usual or any other duty. Richardson provides examples of work-related accidents or mishaps (that occurred during the
member’s regular or assigned duties) that qualify for accidental disability, such as a teacher tripping over a bleacher (as akin to
the present case); a librarian being hit by a falling bookshelf; or a social worker catching her hand in the car door while
transporting a child. Each of these examples demonstrates the Supreme Court’s new vision of the types of work-related
accidents or mishaps that might be eligible for accidental-disability retirement benefits. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213–14.
The Court’s illustrations involve simple accidents or unanticipated mishaps that occur during the member’s work-related
assignments.
By letter dated October 17, 2013, the Board determined that petitioner failed to satisfy the “undesigned and unexpected”
prong (2b) of the “traumatic event” criterion (2) of the Richardson standard, and not the “regular or assigned duties” criterion (3).
The Board’s denial letter to petitioner states, “the event that caused your disability claim is not undesigned or unexpected.” (J-4.)
The Board’s comment suggests or implies that because petitioner was performing his regular or assigned duties and because
“there was no accident or external happening,” petitioner is ineligible for accidental-disability retirement benefits. (J-4.) The
Board holds (and has held) that if the member is performing his regular or assigned duties the incident cannot be undesigned
4
and unexpected. If this were true, no member would ever qualify for accidental disability, because the member must be injured
while performing his regular or assigned duties under Richardson. The Board, in its closing submission, parses or mis-applies
Richardson to the facts of this case and asserts that “work effort itself . . . cannot be the traumatic event.” (Resp’t’s Br. at 13,
quoting Parker-Rogers v. PFRS, No. A-0921-13T1 (App. Div. June 23, 2015), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>.) The
full Richardson quote, in context, provides:
We return again to our case law, which, instead of constituting a single plait, is comprised of two
distinct strands. We denominate the first strand as the Cattani strand. It includes Hillman, Russo,
Cattani, Gerba, Korelnia, and Gable. That strand recognizes the limited purpose underlying the
statutory amendments (to exclude Dwyer and Fattore); declares that, where the disability arises
out of a combination of pre-existing disease and work effort, a traumatic event has not
occurred; underscores that what is required is a force or cause external to the worker (not
pre-existing disease) that directly results in injury; and identifies ordinary mishaps,
including lacerations, trips, and falls, as traumatic events. That strand reaffirms that a

[5]
traumatic event can occur during usual work effort, but that work effort itself or combined with
pre-existing disease cannot be the traumatic event.
[Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 211 (emphasis added).]
Indeed, the Richardson Court supported its decision with specific illustrations depicting how a work-related accident, i.e., work
effort alone, can be the traumatic event.
By way of example, a police officer who has a heart attack while chasing a suspect has not
experienced a traumatic event. In that case, the work effort, alone or in combination with pre-existing
disease, was the cause of the injury. However, the same police officer, permanently and totally
disabled during the chase because of a fall, has suffered a traumatic event. Similarly, the gym
teacher who develops arthritis from the repetitive effects of his work over the years has not suffered
a traumatic event. His disability is the result of degenerative disease and is not related to an event
that is identifiable as to time and place. On the contrary, the same gym teacher who trips over a
riser and is injured has satisfied the standard.
[Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213 (emphasis added).]
The Board’s position has evolved over the last few years, and its decisions seem to be attempting a gradual rewrite or erosion
of the Richardson standard, so that accidents arising from the work effect alone, even without a pre-existing condition, are
excluded from accidental-disability consideration. In my view, such a holding or gradual erosion conflicts with the intent and spirit
of Richardson.
Under Richardson, the member must establish that he was performing his regular or assigned duties in order to qualify for
accidental-disability retirement benefits. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13, criterion 3. Indeed, petitioner here was
performing his school duties by accompanying and supervising the non-swimming students who were sitting in the bleachers. (J-
2.) A fire alarm rang and the students had to be escorted down the bleachers and out of the pool area across a wet tile floor. I
CONCLUDE that petitioner was injured while performing his regular or assigned duties, satisfying Richardson criterion 3, which
the Board does not dispute.
Under Richardson, the member must next establish that while performing his regular or assigned duties, he suffered a
traumatic event. A traumatic event has three elements: (2a) “identifiable as to time and place”; (2b) “undesigned and
unexpected”; and (2c) “caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease that is
aggravated or accelerated by the work).” Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13. These elements all relate to qualifying the
unanticipated mishap (i.e., accident) for accidental-disability retirement benefits.
The Board here does not challenge prong 2a, “identifiable as to time and place.” The Board does, however, challenge
prongs 2b and 2c, denying accidental disability based on its determination that the event was not “undesigned and unexpected”
and that there was no “external happening.” (J-4.) But an external happening alone is not part of the Richardson criteria or the
statute. The actual language in Richardson states: “2.c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of
pre-existing disease that is aggravated or accelerated by the work).” Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13 (emphasis
added). Thus, the Board misinterprets prong 2c and narrowly construes or limits accidental-disability claims to external events,
ignoring the parenthetical explanation delineating the clear meaning of the term “external to the member.” See Moran, supra, 438
N.J. Super. at 353 (holding, “[w]e conclude that the Board’s decision misread Richardson, misapplied the statute, and took an

unduly narrow view of what constitutes an ‘unexpected and undesigned’ traumatic event”). Clearly, the Richardson Court was
excluding accidents and injuries that involve pre-existing diseases such as arthritis, heart conditions, and degenerative
diseases, and exacerbation of pre-existing injuries. The Richardson Court also made clear that ordinary accidents (e.g.,
“unanticipated mishaps,” as unmistakably explained by the Court) that occur on the job are eligible for accidental-disability
benefits. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213. Here, the Board transposed “caused by a circumstance external to the member”
with “external happening.” (J-4.) Indeed, the Richardson Court was, under prong 2c, limiting accidental-disability benefits when
the accident was due to “pre-existing disease that is aggravated or accelerated by the work.” Richardson did not hold that an
accident had to involve an “external happening,” as used by the Board and in some unreported appellate cases. Richardson
articulated a simple standard: “[t]hus, a member who is injured as a direct result of an identifiable, unanticipated mishap has
satisfied the traumatic event standard.” Ibid. (emphasis added). I CONCLUDE that petitioner was injured in an accident
caused by circumstances external to him, and that the accident was not the result of pre-existing disease that was aggravated or
accelerated by the work, satisfying Richardson prong 2c.
Therefore, petitioner is left only with establishing whether the accident was “undesigned and unexpected.” Richardson,
supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13. Here, it is plainly obvious that petitioner experienced an unanticipated mishap when he slipped and
fell on the wet pool deck, during a fire drill, while he was escorting students from the area. These circumstances are equally, if not
more, “unexpected and undesigned” than those of the hypothetical examples noted in Richardson of members who would qualify
for accidental disability (a teacher who trips over a bleacher; a librarian who is hit by a falling bookshelf; or a social worker who
catches her hand in the car door while transporting a child). Petitioner was at significantly greater risk of injury when he stepped
off the bleachers onto a wet pool deck during a fire drill than the clumsy teacher who fell over the bleachers or the inattentive
social worker who closed a car door on her hand. Paradoxically, Richardson holds that the clumsy teacher recovers accidental
disability, while the Board in this case holds that a teacher at greater risk of injury must be denied accidental disability. As will be
more fully discussed below, the phrase “undesigned and unexpected” must be given the meaning intended by the Court in
Richardson. I CONCLUDE that the event suffered by petitioner was undesigned and unexpected, satisfying Richardson prong
2b.
To summarize, petitioner was totally and permanently disabled as a result of an on-the-job accident or “unanticipated
6
mishap” (i.e., traumatic event ) while performing his regular or assigned duties. Petitioner’s injury was caused by circumstances
external to him, and the permanent injury was not the result of pre-existing disease that was aggravated or accelerated by the
work. This is precisely what Richardson requires petitioner to prove, and petitioner has met his burden of proof. I so
CONCLUDE.
Recently reported appellate-court decisions support the above conclusions. In Brooks v. Board of Trustees, PERS, TYP
02426-10 Initial Decision (January 28, 2011), aff’d, Bd. of Trs. (March 17, 2011), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/>, the
Board, in adopting the administrative law judge (ALJ’s) Initial Decision, reasoned that an accident that results from purposeful or
intentional acts is not undesigned and unexpected. Brooks involved a school custodian moving a 300-pound weight bench with
the help of some students. The bench was suddenly and unexpectedly dropped by the students. The custodian was totally and
permanently injured due to spinal herniation(s).
The ALJ and the Board focused on the member’s job duties, and concluded that since the accident occurred as part of
the member’s normal work activity it had to be designed and expected, and therefore accidental disability must be denied. The
language “normal work activity” was juxtaposed with “undesigned and unexpected” to reach this result. This was not the intended
interpretation envisioned by the Supreme Court in Richardson. Indeed, “undesigned and unexpected” falls under a prong, 2b, of
the “traumatic event” criterion, 2, while “regular or assigned duties” is a separate stand-alone criterion, 3, in Richardson.
Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13. These are independent criteria that do not amplify, modify or impact upon each other.
Under the Board’s rationale, the majority of work-related accidents would be excluded from accidental disability, because
accidents generally occur during normal work activities, and all work activity is purposeful, designed and expected. Indeed, the
statute states that the member will “be retired by the board of trustees, if [the] employee is permanently and totally disabled as a

7
direct result of [an accident ] occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or assigned duties, on an
8
accidental disability allowance.” N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43. It is simply the occurrence of an “accident” during work that qualifies for
the disability program. On this point the Richardson Court clearly explained:
In sum, the fact that a member is injured while performing his ordinary duties does not disqualify him
from receiving accidental disability benefits; some injuries sustained during ordinary work effort will
pass muster and others will not. The polestar of the inquiry is whether, during the regular
performance of his job, an unexpected happening, not the result of pre-existing disease alone or
in combination with the work, has occurred and directly resulted in the permanent and total disability
of the member.
X.
In this case, the Board conceded from the beginning that Richardson was permanently and totally
disabled as the direct result of a work-related incident. The only contested issue was whether that
incident constituted a traumatic event. Given the clarified test for traumatic event expressed above
and our discussion of work effort, Richardson satisfied the accidental disability statute. While
performing the regular tasks of his job as a corrections officer, subduing an inmate,
Richardson was thrown to the floor and hyperextended his wrist. As a direct result, he became
permanently and totally disabled. The occurrence was (a) identifiable as to time and place; (b)
unexpected and undesigned; and (c) not caused by a pre-existing condition of Richardson, alone or
in combination with work effort. In short, Richardson suffered a traumatic event.
[Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213–14 (emphasis added).]
The Appellate Division reversed the Board in Brooks. The Appellate Division observed in Brooks that
[t]he ALJ, whose recommended decision the Board adopted, reasoned that because appellant took
charge of carrying the weight bench into the gymnasium with the assistance of the students, he
should have anticipated the dangers involved in this work, including the risk that the bench would fall
on his foot, and therefore, his accident was not “undesigned and unexpected.” However, it could as
well be said that a librarian who re-shelves books should reasonably anticipate that if this activity is
not conducted properly, the book shelf could fall, that a social worker who transports a child to court
should anticipate that if she is not careful getting into or out of her car, she could catch her hand in
the car door, and that a gym teacher who does not look at the ground while walking should anticipate
that he or she could trip on a riser or other object. Yet the Court recognized that such work-
connected accidents could constitute “traumatic events.” Thus, it is clear that an accident can
be “undesigned and unexpected” under the Richardson tests even though it may be concluded in
retrospect that the employee could have anticipated the risk of such an accident and taken steps to
avoid it.
A public employee who is totally and permanently disabled as a direct result of a traumatic event
occurring in the course of employment is disqualified from receiving an accidental disability
pension only if the traumatic event resulted from the “member’s willful negligence.” N.J.S.A.
43:15A-43. Consequently, the fact that an employee’s simple negligence may have been a
contributing cause of an accident is not disqualifying. An applicant for an accidental disability
pension only has to show that he or she suffered a total and permanently disabling injury “as a direct
result of an identifiable, unanticipated mishap,” 192 N.J. at 213, 927 A.2d 543, even though the
employee’s conduct may have contributed to that mishap.
[Brooks v. Bd. of Trs., PERS, 425 N.J. Super. 277, 284–85 (App. Div. 2012) (emphasis added)
(footnote omitted).]

It is abundantly clear from Richardson and Brooks, which are the two reported leading authoritative cases, that a member
who is performing his regular or assigned duties cannot be excluded from accidental-disability consideration merely because he
is performing his “regular or assigned duties.” Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212. In fact, the Richardson decision and the
pension statute provide that the incident must occur during the member’s regular or assigned duties to be eligible for an
accidental-disability pension. Ibid.; N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7. And the incident only has to be an “unexpected happening,”
“unanticipated mishap” or “accident” to be a traumatic event. To exclude a member from eligibility because he was performing
his assigned duties is illogical, given the statute’s design and the holdings in Richardson and Brooks.
The Supreme Court did not insert a condition or reservation under the “regular or assigned duties” criterion. Richardson,
supra, 192 N.J. at 213. In fact, the hypothetical school teacher and social worker were arguably negligent. And even in cases
where the member is negligent, the member may recover under the accidental-disability pension program according to
Richardson so long as the member was not willfully negligent (i.e., a heightened level of negligence such as deliberately or
recklessly). (See footnote 2); Brooks, supra, 425 N.J. Super. at 285. In 2012, Brooks reaffirmed the notion that ordinary
accidents, “unanticipated mishaps” or “unexpected happenings,” are the legal equivalent of “traumatic events,” and if they occur
during a member’s regular or assigned duties the member is eligible for accidental-disability retirement.
Indeed, “undesigned” and “unexpected” are terms of art that were inserted by the Supreme Court in Richardson. The
words are to be given their intended meaning in the context and structure as presented in that case. And these terms were
inserted specifically under the second prong (2b) of the traumatic-event criterion (2) of the pension standard in Richardson.
These terms deal with whether the member contrived or manufactured his injury. They have no bearing on or relevance to
“regular or assigned duties,” as this term falls under the third criterion (3) of the Richardson pension standard. The Supreme
Court did not intend the phrase “undesigned and unexpected” to be used to modify or explain what is, or is not, part of a
member’s regular or assigned duties. If this was the Court’s intention it would have included these very important terms of art
under criterion 3, and not prong 2b of criterion 2.
“Unexpected” is defined as “happening without warning; not expected.” Black’s Law Dictionary 1667 (9th ed. 2009).
“Undesigned” is defined as “unintentional or not designed.” Collins English Dictionary (2003). The ordinary definitions have no
correlation to job duties. Rather, the ordinary definitions deal with the element of surprise, lack of notice or awareness, shock,
unforeseen or unpredicted happenings. The Supreme Court used “unexpected happening” or “unanticipated mishap” to define
“undesigned and unexpected.” Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213.
With the assistance of the definitions combined with the Supreme Court’s illustrations, it is apparent that the Supreme
Court intended to deny recovery of accidental disability when the accident was “intentional and designed” (i.e., contrived, part of
the member’s gross neglect), or part of a pre-existing condition, and to authorize accidental-type recovery when the accident
otherwise occurs “without warning.” This is a logical and rational reading of the Richardson Court’s intent based upon the unique
language utilized in Richardson, the organizational structure of the revised paradigm, the clear examples provided therein, and
the recent interpretation by the Appellate Division in Brooks.
The Supreme Court (Richardson) and the Appellate Division (Brooks) have weighed in on this subject with clear guidance in
reported decisions that require no further interpretation. These rulings are binding on the trial courts. I n Jersey City
Redevelopment Agency v. Mack Props. Co. No. 3, 280 N.J. Super. 553, 562 (App. Div. 1995), the Appellate Division stated, “It
is the responsibility of a trial court to comply with the pronouncements of an appellate court. Daniel v. State, Dep’t of Transp.,
239 N.J. Super. 563, 582, 571 A.2d 1329 (App. Div.), certif. denied, 122 N.J. 325, 585 A.2d 343 (1990).” The trial courts have,
in my opinion, embarked on a path to over-complicate Richardson by defining “undesigned and unexpected” outside of its
simple and basic definition.

I am mindful that under the pre-Richardson paradigm, ordinary slip-and-fall injuries and ordinary accidents occurring on
the job were excluded from accidental disability. The member had to establish that the accident resulted from a great rush of
force or uncontrollable power, which eliminated many cases. These proofs made accidental disability much more difficult to
achieve. But the Richardson decision did away with these confusing and arduous requirements, opening up accidental-disability
claims to a multitude of members who are permanently injured from ordinary job-related accidents (e.g., a social worker who
closes a car door on her hand, or a gym teacher who trips over a bleacher).
Richardson ushered in a major course correction in accidental-disability matters. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 210. For
over forty years, the trial courts and appellate courts applied the “great rush of force and uncontrollable power” criteria to define
what a traumatic event was. Hundreds, if not thousands, of cases were heard, denying or granting members eligibility under the
wrong criteria. The Richardson Court sought to clarify and simplify the definition of traumatic event consistent with the legislative
intent.
Post-Richardson, trial courts are confronting the same difficulties as in the pre-Richardson era, but under the new
paradigm with the terminology “undesigned and unexpected.” Almost identical facts and circumstances are being micro-
analyzed and distinguished under razor-thin differences resulting in varied outcomes.
For example, one line of cases involves lifting/pushing accidents. These include a police officer lifting a traffic-control
trailer, a correction officer lifting a paralyzed inmate from his wheelchair, a maintenance worker lifting a weight bench, a
maintenance worker lifting snow while shoveling, a maintenance worker lifting a heavy trash receptacle, and a police officer
pushing a car stranded in the snow. The disposition in all of these cases turns, in part, on the interpretation of “undesigned and
unexpected.”
In Brooks, the Appellate Division held that the member was eligible for accidental-disability benefits when he injured his
back while lifting the weight bench. In Gibson v. PFRS, TYP 16431-12, Initial Decision (November 28, 2014),a ff’d, Bd. of Trs.
(January 13, 2015), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/>, a police officer was lifting and unhooking a traffic-signage trailer
from the police vehicle when he herniated spinal discs at C5-6 and C6-7. The PFRS Board affirmed the ALJ and approved the
member for accidental disability. In Weinlein v. PFRS, TYP 9736-12, Initial Decision (November 10, 2014),a ff’d, Bd. of Trs.
(December 9, 2014), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/>, a police officer injured his left arm and shoulder when, in the
performance of his duties, he pushed a snow-stuck car that lurched forward and caused him to fall. The PFRS Board affirmed
the ALJ and approved the member for accidental disability.
Conversely, in Parker-Rodgers v. PFRS, supra, No. A-0921-13T1 (App. Div. June 23, 2015),
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>, the Appellate Division denied accidental disability where a correction officer lifted a
250-pound inmate out of a wheelchair, injuring his back. The panel determined that it was part of the normal work effort and not
undesigned or unexpected. Likewise, in Ciallella v. Board of Trustees, PERS, No. A-0344-10 (App. Div. July 26, 2011),
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>, the appellate panel held that a sanitation worker who was injured while dumping the
contents of a heavy trash can into a truck was not entitled to accidental disability benefits because the work activity was not
“undesigned and unexpected.” I n Clayton v. PERS, No. A-1098-12T4 (March 28, 2014),
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>, the panel denied accidental-disability benefits where a maintenance worker
claimed that his disability was due to injuries to his back, legs, and feet as a direct result of a snow-shoveling incident.
All of the aforementioned cases have countless similarities and few differences. The essential and common thread is that
they involve very similar work-related lifting or pushing incidents, resulting in permanent disabilities. A member that lifts a weight

bench or lifts a traffic-signage trailer receives accidental-disability benefits, while a member that lifts an inmate from a
wheelchair or lifts heavy snow while shoveling snow is denied benefits. There is no discernible line of separation. The same
analysis could be made in police/firemen training-exercises cases.
The phrase “undesigned and unexpected” has replaced “great rush of force and uncontrollable power” in presenting a
new quandary for consistently and fairly deciding accidental-disability cases.
If the Board desires to amend or change the accidental-disability standard it must do so through proper rulemaking or
legislation. Metromedia, Inc. v. Dir., Div. of Taxation, 97 N.J. 313 (1984). Trying to amend or modify the Richardson standard
through administrative adjudications that conflict with Richardson denies members proper notice and due process.
I CONCLUDE that petitioner meets the elements of the accidental-disability statute when “accident” is substituted for
“traumatic event.” Petitioner was “permanently and totally disabled as a direct result of [an accident] occurring during and as a
result of the performance of his regular or assigned duties.” N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43.
I further CONCLUDE that petitioner’s lumbar-back injury was “undesigned and unexpected,” as it resulted from petitioner
experiencing an “unexpected happening,” “unanticipated mishap” or “accident” (i.e., traumatic event) that occurred while he was
performing his regular or assigned duties. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13. Stated differently, the injury was not designed
and expected to occur when petitioner was supervising the students at the swimming pool. Petitioner met the Richardson
standard and proved he suffered a career-ending injury that occurred during work-related tasks. The Board cannot use the fact
that the petitioner affirmatively proved that he was performing his regular or assigned duties under Richardson criterion 3, and
thereafter determine that he is ineligible for accidental-disability benefits because he was performing his regular or assigned
duties (holding that accidents that occur during performance of one’s regular or assigned duties are part of the normal work
effort and therefore not undesigned and unexpected). This type of holding is circuitous, and pits the Richardson criteria against
itself (Richardson criterion 3, if proven, negates prong 2b of criterion 2). This is not what Richardson holds or intends, as is so
clearly illustrated by the hypothetical work-related accidents, to wit: a teacher tripping over a bleacher; a librarian being hit by a
falling bookshelf; or a social worker catching her hand in the car door while transporting a child. Each of these examples involves
someone who was performing his or her regular or assigned duties, and because of a work-related accident or unanticipated
mishap that occurred during the performance of those regular or assigned duties, sustained a totally and permanently disabling
career-ending injury that qualified the employee for accidental-disability retirement benefits. The same standard applies to this
petitioner.
ORDER
For the reasons expressed above, I ORDER that the determination of the Board of Trustees of the PERS beR EVERSED.
Petitioner is GRANTED accidental-disability retirement benefits.
